Nepal Floods 2026 Explained: What Caused the Deadly Flash Flood? On August 26, 2026, a deadly flash flood struck the Himalayas along the border of Nepal and Tibet, causing devastating loss of life and wiping out vital infrastructure. While initial reports blamed an earthquake or a Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF), satellite analysis revealed a far more terrifying reality: a massive 600-meter glacier block detached and fell 1,200 meters straight down. In this full-length documentary, we break down the physics, geography, and political failures behind the disaster. The friction of millions of tons of rock and ice falling at highway speeds pulverized the glacier into water in mid-air, creating a temporary debris dam in the Lhende Khola river. When the dam burst, the mud and rock slurry acted like "wet concrete," sweeping downstream toward the Rasuwagadhi border crossing. #nepal #nepalflood #nepalnews #himalayas #tibet

More than 1,300 people are missing in Nepal and Tibet, including 47 Americans, after a glacial collapse caused catastrophic floods, with video showing mud sweeping through entire communities. Drone footage in Nepal showed roads destroyed and buildings buried by thundering water the color of wet cement. Nepalese authorities ramped up operations in the worst-affected districts of Nuwakot and Rasuwa. The disaster in Nepal and Tibet is not a one-off. The Lhende Khola river system has now flooded twice in just 14 months and the increasingly unstable Himalayan ice system threatens communities, infrastructure and water supplies across one of the world’s most densely populated regions. The region saw similar flash floods in August last year, when a glacial lake in Tibet overflowed because of high temperatures. Nine people were killed, and critical infrastructure, including a bridge connecting Nepal and China, was damaged.

videos.caption: The office of Nepal's energy minister says two people have been rescued alive from a hydropower tunnel nine days after floods hit the area. Earlier on Friday, Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha's office said in a statement the two workers pulled from the tunnel at the Upper Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station are Sanjay Sah, a mechanical foreman, and Kabir Maharjan, a mechanical supervisor. Mr Maharjan cannot move his hands and legs but Mr Sah's injuries are not critical, an aide to the energy minister told Reuters news agency. The two are being taken to a hospital in Kathmandu, he said. The rescues come nine days after the August 26 floods, likely caused by a glacier collapse, that devastated towns and valleys in Nepal. At least 1,259 people were killed and more than 5,000 remain missing, according to the country's disaster management agency. China, as of late Wednesday, said 21 people were killed and 541 were missing on the Tibet side of the border. About 900 workers are missing from 12 hydropower projects in Nepal, with roughly 500 believed to be trapped in tunnels, according to local authorities. #Nepal #ABCNews

The 2026 Nepal Flood Explained: Where Did All The Water Come From? (Part 1) On August 26, 2026, a catastrophic flash flood struck the Nepal-Tibet border, erasing infrastructure in a terrifying 13-minute window. Initial global reports blamed a simple earthquake or a glacial lake outburst—but satellite imagery and seismic data proved both theories completely wrong. In Part 1 of this forensic scientific investigation, we solve the central mystery: Where did millions of cubic meters of water suddenly originate in a valley with no lake? We analyze the 34-million-year-old metamorphic bedrock failure on Langtang Lirung at 5,200 meters, the physics of kinetic friction melting, the impact that pulverized a hidden lower-valley glacier, and how the resulting wave reached 160 km/h.
